fixes.explanation: Close, but it's the other way around. The people left in Jerusalem fall with the bad figs, because the LORD says, "But like the bad figs, so bad they cannot be eaten… so will I deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the remnant of Jerusalem…" (Jeremiah 24:8) Zedekiah is the king of Judah in this part. The good figs are the exiles, the ones who were sent away. It's a surprise, and I think plenty of folks would pick Jerusalem first.

This comparison doesn't name the priests separately. The LORD says, "Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah…" (Jeremiah 24:5) The baskets sat in front of the temple, but the good figs are the exiles. Don't let the location fool you, friend.

Yes, baker. God says, "I will build them up and not tear them down…" (Jeremiah 24:6) Building up is the opposite of tearing down, and He says both out loud. I've been torn down and built back up myself, and building is the better deal. Sharp work.

Sacrifices aren't the reason God gives. He says, "They will be My people, and I will be their God, for they will return to Me with all their heart." (Jeremiah 24:7) The reason is their return with all their heart. Sacrifices don't come up in this verse, friend, and neither does a to-do list.

Moab isn't named here. The verse says, "…the remnant of Jerusalem—those remaining in this land and those living in the land of Egypt." (Jeremiah 24:8) Egypt is the place on the list, so that's the one to remember. Moab is a fair guess, friend, but the verse goes down to Egypt.

Right, baker. God says He'll make them "…a disgrace and an object of scorn, ridicule, and cursing wherever I have banished them." (Jeremiah 24:9) This one is heavy, so I'll just say it plainly. Scorn is the word, and you caught it.

Praise isn't the word in this verse. The verse says, "…a disgrace and an object of scorn, ridicule, and cursing wherever I have banished them." (Jeremiah 24:9) The word is scorn. This is a heavy part of the passage, friend.
